title: The estimated mean of the leading minimum wage arm
published: The winning arm, by a hair, was Proposal 3 ([[B]], without current minimum wage), with a probability of being best of 0.219 and an estimated mean of [[0.895]] over 183 respondents.
corrected: The winning arm, by a hair, was Proposal 3 ([[N]], without current minimum wage), with a probability of being best of 0.219 and an estimated mean of [[0.865]] over 183 respondents.
note: The arm with a 0.219 probability of being best and 183 respondents is Proposal 3 (N), whose inverse-probability-weighted mean is 0.865. The 0.895 printed in the sentence is Figure 4's estimate for Proposal 3 (Y), a different arm, which drew 121 respondents and ended with a 0.120 probability of being best. Figures 3 and 4 label the two versions of each minimum wage proposal "(Y)" and "(N)", so the "B" in the parenthesis is also an "N".

title: The arm carrying the 4.1-point Republican effect
published: In this particular case, the adaptive design with the smaller standard error allows us to declare the 4.1-point average effect of the [[accuracy]] treatment statistically significant (p = 0.014), whereas under that static design the effect would not have attained statistical significance (p = 0.152).
corrected: In this particular case, the adaptive design with the smaller standard error allows us to declare the 4.1-point average effect of the [[Lottery]] treatment statistically significant (p = 0.014), whereas under that static design the effect would not have attained statistical significance (p = 0.152).
note: Figure 6 gives the Republican Lottery arm an effect of 4.1 percentage points with a p-value of 0.014. The Accuracy arm's Republican estimate is -5.3 percentage points, in the opposite direction, with a p-value of 0.314. The two preceding sentences and Figure 5 both identify the Lottery as the arm in question. The static-design p-value of 0.152 is left as printed: it comes from a bootstrap the deposited materials do not seed reproducibly, and the reproduction cannot recompute it.

title: The share of static minimum wage simulations picking the best proposal
published: Treating observed success rates as the truth in simulations of the minimum wage experiment, we picked the best proposal 47% of the time in adaptive experiments and [[37%]] of the time in static experiments.
corrected: Treating observed success rates as the truth in simulations of the minimum wage experiment, we picked the best proposal 47% of the time in adaptive experiments and [[36.5%]] of the time in static experiments.
note: The deposited simulations pick the best minimum wage proposal in 36.46 per cent of 10,000 static runs, which is 36 per cent at the whole-percentage precision the sentence uses. Rounding to one decimal first gives 36.5, and rounding that again gives 37. The other three shares in the same passage round correctly.

title: The two randomization inference p-values are transposed
published:
Using randomization inference, we reject the null of no difference across treatments (p = [[0.028]]).

Using randomization inference, we again reject the null (p = [[0.013]]).
corrected:
Using randomization inference, we reject the null of no difference across treatments (p = [[0.015]]).

Using randomization inference, we again reject the null (p = [[0.021]]).
note:
The first sentence is about the Republican trial and the second about the Democratic one. Run on the deposited data, the deposit's own script returns the published pair with the parties exchanged: 0.013 for the Republicans and 0.028 for the Democrats. The observed F statistics settle which way round it belongs: the Republican F is 2.31 against the Democratic 1.93, and the larger F takes the smaller p-value, so the smaller of the two p-values is the Republicans'. Both nulls are still rejected at conventional levels and no conclusion changes; only the two numbers swap places.

The corrected values are this reproduction's own, from a seeded run of the deposited procedure at 1,000 iterations. They differ in the third decimal from the deposit's unseeded run, which is the sampling variation the procedure carries.

title: The independence that warrants the Horvitz-Thompson factorisation names the realized outcome
note: The realized outcome is $Y_i = \sum_k \mathbf{1}\{K_i = k\} Y_i(k)$, a deterministic function of the assignment and the potential outcomes, so it is never independent of $K_i$ given $S_i$ once treatment has an effect. The condition the proof needs is independence of the *potential* outcome, $Y_i(k) \perp\!\!\!\perp K_i \mid S_i$, which is what B.2 assumes two paragraphs earlier and what B.3 assumes again. The expression being factored on this line already carries $Y_i(k)$ rather than $Y_i$, so the step is valid and only its stated warrant is wrong. No other line of B.2 is affected and the unbiasedness result stands.

title: The variance of the control-augmented estimator drops the covariance between its two terms
published: $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat\tau_k^{HT} \mid S_i\right] = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}\left[Y_i(k) \frac{\mathbf{1}\{K_i = k\}}{\pi_i(k; S_i)} \;\middle|\; S_i\right] + \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}\left[Y_i(0) \frac{\mathbf{1}\{K_i = 0\}}{\pi_i(0; S_i)} \;\middle|\; S_i\right]$
corrected: $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat\tau_k^{HT} \mid S_i\right] = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}\left[Y_i(k) \frac{\mathbf{1}\{K_i = k\}}{\pi_i(k; S_i)} \;\middle|\; S_i\right] + \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}\left[Y_i(0) \frac{\mathbf{1}\{K_i = 0\}}{\pi_i(0; S_i)} \;\middle|\; S_i\right]$ [[$+\; \frac{2}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \Pr[Y_i(k) = 1] \Pr[Y_i(0) = 1]$]]
note:
$\hat\tau_k^{HT}$ is a difference of two Horvitz-Thompson means, so its variance carries $-2\operatorname{Cov}$ and the display is a sum of two variances with nothing in that place. The covariance does not vanish. Within a unit the two indicators are mutually exclusive, so the product of the two terms is identically zero and their conditional covariance is $-\Pr[Y_i(k) = 1]\Pr[Y_i(0) = 1]$, which enters the variance with the opposite sign. The printed expression therefore understates the variance by the term shown. 

 **Neither conclusion drawn from the display moves.** The missing term is free of the assignment probabilities, so it leaves the minimisation untouched: minimising $\Pr[Y_i(k) = 1]/\pi_i(k; S_i) + \Pr[Y_i(0) = 1]/\pi_i(0; S_i)$ at fixed total probability still gives probabilities proportional to the square roots of the success rates, and the comparison against the static design at $1/(K+1)$ still favours the adaptive design for $K > 1$. Entry 8 corrects the same display's conditioning and the two compose: the term added here is the one that survives into the unconditional variance entry 8 states.

title: The variance display conditions on one unit's history while summing over all of them
published: [[Conditional on history, the]] variance can be expressed as, [[$\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat\tau_k^{HT} \mid S_i\right]$]]$\; = \;$ $\frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}\left[\,\cdot\,\middle|\; S_i\right] + \cdots$
corrected: [[Because the summands are a martingale difference sequence with respect to the history, the]] variance can be expressed as, [[$\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat\tau_k^{HT}\right]$]]$\; = \;$ $\frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathrm{E}\operatorname{Var}\left[\,\cdot\,\middle|\; S_i\right] + \cdots$
note:
The index $i$ is free on the left of the printed equality and bound by the sum on the right. Neither reading of the conditioning supports the display. Conditioning on one unit's history cannot license summing per-unit variances, because under adaptive assignment the units are dependent; conditioning on the whole history leaves only the last unit random, and the sum collapses to a single term. 

 **The sum-of-variances structure is nonetheless right, for the unconditional variance.** Under the constant means the section assumes, $\mathrm{E}$ of each summand given the history is the constant $\tau_k$, so the centred summands are a martingale difference sequence and every cross-unit covariance is zero. What the section needs is that argument rather than a conditioning bar. The right-hand side is abbreviated above because entry 7 is what changes it; the two entries mark disjoint spans of one display and are applied together.

title: "The product of two binomials is also a binomial"
published: The $Y_i(k)$ and $\mathbf{1}\{K_i = k\}$ terms are independent [[binomials]], and the product of two [[binomials]] is also a [[binomial]], and so we express the variance of their product accordingly.
corrected: The $Y_i(k)$ and $\mathbf{1}\{K_i = k\}$ terms are independent [[Bernoullis]], and the product of two [[Bernoullis]] is also a [[Bernoulli]], and so we express the variance of their product accordingly.
note: As a claim about the binomial distribution the sentence is false: the product of two $\text{Binomial}(n, p)$ variables with $n > 1$ is not binomial. It holds for the Bernoulli case, which is the only one used here and the one the section's constant-means assumption sets up, and the display that follows is correct. Writing $p = \Pr[Y_i(k) = 1 \mid S_i]$ and $q = \Pr[K_i = k \mid S_i]$, the product is $\text{Bernoulli}(pq)$ with variance $pq(1 - pq)$, which is what is printed. Only the word is wrong.

title: "ams" for "arms"
published: They show regret as a function of the expected sum of assignments to suboptimal arms, multiplied by the difference between the best arm mean and the mean under [[ams]] $k \neq k^{*}$.
corrected: They show regret as a function of the expected sum of assignments to suboptimal arms, multiplied by the difference between the best arm mean and the mean under [[arms]] $k \neq k^{*}$.
note: A dropped letter. The sentence is otherwise right, and so is the claim it leads to: the expected number of plays of suboptimal arms under Thompson sampling grows as $O(\ln N)$ against $O(N)$, that being $N/(K+1)$, under a random design.

title: Arm two's posterior density carries arm one's parameters
note:
The inner integral is arm two's posterior density. Its normalising constant $c_{2,t}$ is indexed correctly and both exponents are not: they carry arm one's parameters. 

 The line immediately below, which substitutes $t = 1$, uses arm two's parameters correctly, $\Gamma(3)/\Gamma(1)\Gamma(2)$ and $\theta_2^{0}(1 - \theta_2)^{1}$, which is the $\text{Beta}(1, 2)$ posterior the preceding paragraph derives for arm two. So the defect is confined to the general display, and the $5/6$ the calculation evaluates to is right.

title: The expected best-arm sample mean is offered as a bias that adaptive assignment introduces
published: If we condition on the best observed arm, however, the expected sample mean of the best arm is 0.708, although the true parameter value for either arm is 0.5.
note:
The number is right. Enumerating the example's sixteen paths returns 0.708, and the two-period enumeration in Table C.1 reproduces in both of its columns. What the number cannot carry is the weight the section puts on it. C.2 exists to show that "this preferential assignment probability conditional on observed success or failure introduces a source of bias into estimation", and both figures in the enumeration are offered under that heading.

The first one earns it. $\mathrm{E}[\hat\theta_k] = 0.458$ against a truth of $0.5$ is exactly the bias the section is about, and a static 50-50 design run through the same enumeration returns 0.500, unbiased. The second one does not. The maximum of two noisy estimates exceeds their common mean under any design whatever, adaptive or not, and the same static 50-50 design returns 0.750 here: **higher** than the 0.708 the adaptive design produces. Read as the section invites, the figure points the wrong way, because more of the second period's probability goes to the arm that is currently ahead, and that arm's mean is the one a failure pulls down.

Nothing is corrected on the page. The sentence states a true number and the defect is in what a reader is invited to conclude from it, which is not a thing an erratum can fix by replacing a token; rewriting the section's framing would be editing the authors' argument rather than correcting their record. The entry stands as a note so that the finding is on the record beside the sentence it concerns. Both comparisons above are computed at render time from the setup C.2 itself states, and the computation is held to reproducing the appendix's own 0.458 and 0.708 before its counterfactual is reported.
